extracted.intended_audience: general readers and students of Montaigne / readers of Renaissance essays
extracted.subtask_description: Close-reading of Montaigne's Essays (selected chapters) focusing on practical-philosophical judgments about conduct (purpose, vices, drunkenness, suicide) rather than prescriptive how-to technical rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Act with a determinate end
rubrics_metrics.description: One ought to know the aim before arranging the parts of a life or undertaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne compares the archer (who must know what to aim at) and the painter (who needs the full form in imagination) to life: counsels and actions deviate when not levelled to a determinate end. 'No wind serves him who addresses his voyage to no certain port.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid judging general capacity from a single action
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not infer a person's overall competence from one work or single appearance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne rejects concluding Sophocles' household skill from reading one tragedy and criticises the Parians who made governors from observing good private housekeeping; such extrapolations are unreliable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Private prudence does not guarantee public competence
rubrics_metrics.description: Good management of private affairs is not conclusive evidence of capacity to govern public matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the Parians who selected governors among provident private farmers, wrongly assuming private thrift equalled public aptitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect human inconsistency and variety
rubrics_metrics.description: People are composite and variable; one should expect differences between a person at different times and between people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne: 'We are all lumps, and of so various and inform a contexture, that every piece plays, every moment, its own game' — this warns against expecting consistent behaviour or identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge actions by underlying motives, not outward appearance alone
rubrics_metrics.description: Understanding a person's motives is necessary to judge actions fairly; outward acts can mislead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne argues that intelligence must 'penetrate the very soul' to discover the springs guiding motion; judging by outward action alone is insufficient and hazardous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish vices by degree and kind
rubrics_metrics.description: Vices are all vices but vary in quality and gravity; one must discriminate among them rather than treat them as equal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne warns against conflating all sins (e.g., treating sacrilege and petty theft as equivalent); failing to distinguish benefits murderers/tyrants who exploit such leveling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drunkenness is a brutish, primarily corporeal vice
rubrics_metrics.description: Drunkenness uniquely overthrows reason and renders the body stupid; unlike some vices, it is chiefly physical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne contrasts drunkenness with vices that mix knowledge and cunning; wine 'totally overthrows' the mind, producing heaviness, torpid tongue, dimmed mind, quarrels, etc. He cites classical authorities (Lucretius, Horace) on effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drunkenness reveals secrets and undermines trust
rubrics_metrics.description: Excessive drinking can make people betray secrets and be unfit for trust-sensitive roles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Josephus' ambassador revealing secrets after being plied with liquor; historical anecdotes of trusted persons being drunk yet entrusted with secrets show both risk and counterexamples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public duties demand abstention or restraint in drinking
rubrics_metrics.description: Judges, magistrates, and those administering public affairs should refrain from drinking when performing their duties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne summarises Plato: magistrates should abstain from excess, not drink on days devoted to public business, and keep nights needed for procreation free from intoxication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation and appropriate timing in drinking
rubrics_metrics.description: Drinking may have place and utility (recreation, restoring gaiety), but it requires moderation and appropriate timing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne records varied ancient opinions (some permit moderate or occasional drunkenness). He notes Plato's age-based rules: no wine for children until eighteen, no drunkenness until forty; also mentions cultural practices (Germans, Persians, ancients) and physician opinions about stimulating digestion occasionally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive fastidiousness about taste when seeking simple pleasures
rubrics_metrics.description: To derive common enjoyment from drinking, one should not be overly delicate in palate or prefer only the best wines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne advises against delicate choice of wines because a refined taste condemns one to drink the worst; a good toper should have an indifferent, free palate—illustrated by Germans who drink indiscriminately to pour down rather than to taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Curb and moderate inclinations rather than attempt total suppression
rubrics_metrics.description: It is sufficient and realistic to curb and moderate desires; total suppression of natural inclinations is not achievable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne stresses human frailty: even the wisest cannot completely prevent natural reactions (fear, shame, etc.); virtues should aim for moderation not impossible constancy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer endurance and civic duty over suicide except under strict limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Suffering and perseverance within one's duties is often more virtuous than ending one's life; suicide is controversial and may be justified only in limited cases per Stoic thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne surveys opinions: Stoics allow a 'reasonable exit' in some circumstances (e.g., opportunely at height of prosperity), but many argue one must not quit life without divine or civic licence. He cites Cleomenes, who saw constancy in living as sometimes more honourable than suicide, and warns against rash or collective self-destruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not despair while hope remains; avoid rash self-destruction
rubrics_metrics.description: Because human affairs can change suddenly, one should not take life merely to evade present troubles while some hope remains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne points to historical examples of rash mass suicides and counsels that 'All the inconveniences in the world are not considerable enough that a man should die to evade them' — endurance may allow an eventual better state.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate extraordinary claims of constancy and virtue with scepticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims of absolute constancy (e.g., Stoic boasts of immunity to fortune) should be regarded with doubt since extreme examples often reflect frenzy or affected posture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne cites Stoic braggadocio and anecdotes of martyrs and philosophers displaying extremes; he suggests such sallies can be expressions of fury, rapture, or phrenzy rather than sober virtue.
